---
title: "The Clearest Reported NDIS Outcome Gains Are in Early Childhood"
description: "After one reassessment, most published NDIS outcome indicators move only a little. The larger gains are concentrated in communication and friendships among young children."
date: "2026-06-10"
date-modified: "2026-10-13"
categories: [ndis, outcomes, disability, australia]
author: "Aydin"
---



The public NDIS outcomes data tells a more restrained story than either “outcomes improved” or “nothing changed”. After one plan reassessment, most published indicators move by only a few percentage points. The clearest gains are concentrated among children before school age—especially communication and friendships—while the typical adult indicator changes by just 1 percentage point.

That distinction matters. These files contain aggregated survey percentages, not participant-level records, comparison groups or sample sizes. They can show where reported outcomes moved; they cannot establish that the NDIS caused the movement.

## Start with the right baseline

The baseline file is often tempting to describe as “current outcomes”. It is not. It records outcomes **when participants entered the Scheme**, for people represented in the June 2026 extract. It is a starting-point profile.

Among adults, the entry picture separates relatively common measures of home and day-to-day choice from much lower economic and community participation. Only 23% had a paid job, 10% volunteered and 9% participated in education, training or skill development at baseline.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
adult_baseline_patterns <- c(
  "choose what they do each day",
  "choose who supports them",
  "feel safe or very safe",
  "did not have any difficulties accessing health services",
  "rate their health as good",
  "actively involved in a community",
  "have a paid job",
  "participate in education, training",
  "volunteer"
)

adult_baseline <- baseline |>
  filter(cohort == "Adults") |>
  filter(str_detect(str_to_lower(outcome), str_c(adult_baseline_patterns, collapse = "|"))) |>
  mutate(
    outcome_short = short_outcome(outcome),
    outcome_short = fct_reorder(outcome_short, baseline_rate)
  )

assert_true(nrow(adult_baseline) == length(adult_baseline_patterns), "The selected adult baseline outcomes changed.")

ggplot(adult_baseline, aes(baseline_rate, outcome_short)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = baseline_rate, yend = outcome_short), colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#246b8e") +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(baseline_rate, accuracy = 1)), hjust = -0.35, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, 0.85), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.03))) +
  labs(x = "Share at Scheme entry", y = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Selected outcomes for adults at NDIS entry, in the data current to 30 June 2026. These are baseline—not current—levels.](index_files/figure-html/adult-baseline-1.png){fig-alt='Dot chart of nine adult outcomes at NDIS entry. Choosing daily activities, choosing supports, and feeling safe at home are relatively common, while paid work, volunteering, and education or training are below one quarter.' width=768}
:::
:::


## Most first-reassessment changes are small

For each outcome, I compare the baseline percentage with the first reassessment percentage for the group recorded as having one reassessment. Three clearly negative indicator types—broad development concerns, inability to access wanted training, and having no friends beyond family or paid staff—are reversed so that positive always means movement in a favourable direction. The two “want more choice and control” indicators are excluded because their direction is ambiguous: wanting more choice can reveal unmet need, greater agency, or both.

Across the 40 direction-classified participant indicators, most movements cluster close to zero. Early childhood has 4 of 5 indicators moving favourably, but it also contains the largest adverse movement. Adult outcomes are flatter: 8 improve, 6 are unchanged and none worsen at the published one-percentage-point precision.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot_reassessment <- reassessment_one |>
  mutate(cohort = factor(cohort, levels = expected_cohorts))

ggplot(plot_reassessment, aes(cohort, adjusted_change)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.10, height = 0, alpha = 0.55, size = 2.2, colour = "#246b8e", seed = 2026) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.48, linewidth = 0.7, colour = "#9b3f2f") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1), breaks = seq(-0.05, 0.15, 0.05)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Favourable change from baseline")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Direction-adjusted change from baseline to first reassessment. Each point is one published outcome; positive values indicate favourable movement. Red bars are medians across indicators, not participant-level effects.](index_files/figure-html/reassessment-distribution-1.png){fig-alt='Dot plot of 40 direction-classified outcome changes by age cohort. Most cluster between zero and three percentage points. Early childhood contains the two largest gains and the largest decline.' width=768}
:::
:::


## The larger movements are concentrated

The largest favourable change is Can communicate what they want for early childhood, up 15 percentage points. The largest adverse change is Fewer broad development concerns for early childhood, down 7 percentage points after accounting for direction.

The chart makes the concentration visible: the two double-digit gains both relate to children before school age. Adult employment, education and volunteering do not show comparable movement after one reassessment.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
largest_movements <- reassessment_one |>
  slice_max(abs(adjusted_change), n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    label = str_c(cohort, ": ", outcome_short),
    label = fct_reorder(label, adjusted_change),
    direction_label = if_else(adjusted_change >= 0, "Favourable", "Adverse")
  )

ggplot(largest_movements, aes(adjusted_change, label, colour = direction_label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey65") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = adjusted_change, yend = label), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = percent(adjusted_change, accuracy = 1)),
    hjust = if_else(largest_movements$adjusted_change >= 0, -0.25, 1.25),
    show.legend = FALSE,
    size = 3.4
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(-0.09, 0.17)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Favourable = "#16735c", Adverse = "#b0433c")) +
  labs(x = "Direction-adjusted change", y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The ten largest absolute movements from baseline to first reassessment. Positive values indicate favourable movement.](index_files/figure-html/largest-movements-1.png){fig-alt='Diverging dot chart of the ten largest outcome movements. Communication and friendships among young children have the largest gains, while broad early-childhood development concerns have the largest adverse movement.' width=768}
:::
:::


## What the data does—and does not—say

These are published aggregate movements, not participant-level effect estimates. They are not uniformly large and they are not spread evenly across ages or domains. The largest favourable movements are in early-childhood communication and friendship or social connection, while broad development concerns move adversely. For adults, the indicators tied to work, learning and community participation remain low at entry and generally change little after one reassessment.

Three limits should shape the interpretation:

- The extract has no participant-level records or sample counts, so uncertainty cannot be calculated.
- The first-reassessment comparison describes the respondents in that published group; it is not a randomised or matched counterfactual.
- Percentages are rounded to whole percentage points. A reported zero change may conceal a smaller movement.

That leaves a useful, narrower conclusion: the public data supports a story of **concentrated early-childhood gains alongside broadly modest movement elsewhere**, not a single verdict on whether “NDIS outcomes” rose or fell.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Sources and reproducibility"}

The analysis uses the NDIA's [baseline and longitudinal participant outcomes datasets](https://dataresearch.ndis.gov.au/datasets/participant-datasets) and their data-rules documents, all current to 30 June 2026. The source files are pinned by size and SHA-256 checksum in `sources.csv`; set `BLOG_REFRESH_DATA=true` to force a fresh download and checksum validation. In the registry, `release_date` records the downloadable asset's Last-Modified date.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
source_manifest |>
  transmute(
    source = dataset,
    source_revision_date = release_date,
    coverage_end,
    file = local_file,
    bytes = comma(bytes),
    sha256_prefix = substr(sha256, 1, 12)
  ) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Source", "Source/revision date", "Coverage end", "Cached file", "Bytes", "SHA-256 prefix"))
```
